title: The emperor's questions
hook: Heraclius questions Abu Sufyan about the Prophet, and Abu Sufyan can't bring himself to lie
carry: even his enemy told the truth

segments.voice: Yesterday, on Umm Salamah's advice, the Prophet said nothing and shaved his own head, and everyone followed. Your line was: do it first. What did you go first on? Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

A trade caravan from Mecca is doing business in Syria during the truce. Abu Sufyan, a leader of the Prophet's opponents in Mecca, is with it. Then a summons arrives. The Roman emperor, Heraclius, wants to question these Arabs, and asks which of them is the closest relative of the man who claims to be a prophet. Abu Sufyan is. So he finds himself in a royal court, with an interpreter, standing in front of an emperor. Behind him the emperor places his own companions, and tells them: if he lies to me, say so. Today: the emperor's questions.
screen: `A CARAVAN IN SYRIA.` → `SUMMONED TO THE EMPEROR.` → `IF HE LIES, SAY SO.`

segments.voice: This report sits in Sahih al-Bukhari, in the chapter on how revelation began, in Abu Sufyan's own telling. Heraclius asks about the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, one plain question at a time. What is his family like among you? Has anyone among you made this claim before him? Do his followers come from the powerful, or the weak? Are they growing or shrinking? Does anyone leave his religion out of resentment? Did you ever accuse him of lying before he made this claim? Does he break his word? What does he tell you to do? And here's the line that makes the story. Abu Sufyan admits that if he hadn't been afraid of his companions reporting him as a liar, he would have lied. But they were right behind him. So he answered straight. He says the only place he could slip in a little doubt was this: we're in a truce with him now, and we don't know what he'll do in it. Then Heraclius goes back through every answer. A man who never lied about people, he reasons, would not start lying about God. The weak are the ones who follow messengers. Messengers don't betray. One answer after another, the enemy's own testimony draws a picture of an honest man. That's the strange gift in this story. Abu Sufyan didn't come to praise anyone. He came cornered, with his own companions at his back, and the truth came out of him anyway.
screen: `ONE PLAIN QUESTION AT A TIME.` · `HE WOULD HAVE LIED, BUT FOR SHAME.` · `ONE SMALL DOUBT SLIPPED IN.` · `THE ANSWERS DRAW AN HONEST MAN.` · then, large: `EVEN HIS ENEMY TOLD THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: The practice: answer truthfully about a rival. Sit, and let your breathing settle. Bring to mind someone you compete with, or simply don't like. A coworker, a sibling, an old friend you fell out with. Now ask yourself a few of the emperor's plain questions about them. Do they keep their word? Do they lie? Answer honestly, the way Abu Sufyan had to, with someone standing behind you. Notice where you'd like to slip in a little doubt. Let the honest answer stand. If you pray, you can ask Allah to keep your tongue truthful about the people you find hard. The bell holds the time.
Heraclius, the Roman emperor who questioned Abu Sufyan about the Prophet, and whose own reasoning, drawn from an enemy's testimony, described an honest man. Today's word.
Your line: even his enemy told the truth. Today, when someone you find hard comes up in conversation, say only what's true about them, including the good. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims read the Heraclius report near the start of Sahih al-Bukhari, and it is retold as an account of the Prophet's character given by someone who was then his opponent.

fork.setup: you're Abu Sufyan, in front of an emperor, asked about your enemy. your companions stand behind you. what do you do?
options: lie, and make him look bad.
answer straight, slipping in one small doubt.
fork.reveal: he answered honestly, afraid of being called a liar, and slipped in only one doubt: we don't know what he'll do in the truce.

original.note: Arabic: Heraclius, the Roman emperor, as he is named in the report.

trapdoor: what you thought: an emperor interviewing a merchant.
what it means: an opponent's honest answers become a witness to the Prophet's character.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari places this report in his opening chapter on how revelation began, told in Abu Sufyan's own words.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 7 (Kitab Bad' al-Wahy, the report of Heraclius)
